title: Reference: Irregular Verbs & Capitals
source: Harvey's Elementary Grammar & Composition (1880), Appendix, pp. 156-160

slides.heading: Irregular Verbs — A Reference
bullets: Irregular verbs do not add -ed; they must be learned by heart.
No change at all:  cut/cut/cut, put/put/put, hit/hit/hit, let/let/let.
Same past and participle:  bring/brought/brought, buy/bought/bought, make/made/made.
All three different:  go/went/gone, see/saw/seen, write/wrote/written, ring/rang/rung.

slides.heading: More Common Irregular Verbs
bullets: begin/began/begun, drink/drank/drunk, sing/sang/sung, swim/swam/swum.
break/broke/broken, choose/chose/chosen, freeze/froze/frozen, speak/spoke/spoken.
eat/ate/eaten, give/gave/given, take/took/taken, know/knew/known.
ride/rode/ridden, throw/threw/thrown, fly/flew/flown, grow/grew/grown.

slides.heading: Unipersonal Verbs
bullets: A Unipersonal Verb asserts an act with no real subject of its own.
The word “it” stands in as an indefinite subject.
Ex. — “It snows.”  “It rains.”  “It seems so.”
Here “it” names nothing in particular — it simply fills the subject’s place.

slides.heading: Capital Letters — The Rules
bullets: Begin every sentence with a capital letter.
Begin every line of poetry with a capital letter.
Capitalize proper names — people, places, days, months:  Maria, Chicago, Monday, July.
The single words I and O are always capitals.

slides.heading: More Capital Rules
bullets: Titles of honor:  President Lincoln, Doctor Smith, Queen Victoria.
Words made from proper names:  American, French, Shakespearean.
Names for God:  God, the Almighty, the Lord.
Words of special importance may be capitalized for emphasis.

slides.heading: Practice — Capital or Small Letter?
slides.instruction: Should each word begin with a capital or a small letter?

items: Give the past and participle of “go.”
Name things that take a capital letter.
Which single words are always capitals?
answers: One that does not add -ed for its past and participle.
One that asserts an act with no real subject, like “It snows.”
Proper names — people, places, days, and months.
